title: Icosapent ethyl (EPA)
disclaimer: Educational summary of public regulatory and scientific sources (EU product information and assessment reports, clinical trial registers, ESC/EAS guidelines), current as of the Vazkepa product information published by the EMA on 13 March 2026. This is not medical advice and not promotional material. Treatment decisions must follow the current official product information and a qualified healthcare professional.

blocks.markdown:
## What icosapent ethyl is

Icosapent ethyl is a highly purified, prescription-only form of **EPA** (eicosapentaenoic acid), an **omega-3 fatty acid** found in fish oil. It isn't a food supplement. The dose is four 998 mg capsules a day: two in the morning and two in the evening, with or after a meal.

This module is built on the **SmPC** (the regulator-approved reference text for prescribers) for Vazkepa. It's authorised across the EU and now held by Recordati in Milan. The basis is the product information that reflects the January 2026 renewal.

## One indication, tightly defined

Vazkepa is approved for one purpose: to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in adults who are already taking a statin and are at high cardiovascular risk. They must have raised **triglycerides** (a type of blood fat), at 1.7 mmol/L or above, and one of two things:

- **Established cardiovascular disease**, meaning known disease of the heart or blood vessels (such as a previous heart attack, stroke or narrowed leg arteries)
- Diabetes plus at least one other cardiovascular risk factor

It isn't approved as a triglyceride-lowering treatment on its own.

## Not really a triglyceride drug

In its main trial, triglycerides fell by 18% on icosapent ethyl and rose by 2% on placebo at one year. That's a modest effect.

The SmPC states that lowering triglycerides seems to explain only a small part of the benefit. The outcome didn't track how far triglycerides or LDL fell. What tracked the outcome most closely was the level of EPA in the blood.

## What it does to heart events

REDUCE-IT followed 8,179 statin-treated patients for a median of 4.9 years. Its main outcome combined five kinds of event into a **MACE** measure (major adverse cardiovascular events): cardiovascular death, heart attack, stroke, artery-opening procedures and hospitalisation for unstable angina.

- **Main outcome:** 17.2% vs 22.0%, HR 0.75 (95% CI 0.68–0.83). That's 25% lower in relative terms and 4.8 percentage points lower in absolute terms.
- **Cardiovascular death:** 4.3% vs 5.2%, HR 0.80 (95% CI 0.66–0.98).
- **Death from any cause:** 6.7% vs 7.6%, HR 0.87 (95% CI 0.74–1.02). Not significant.

## What to watch

- **Bleeding:** 11.8% vs 9.9%. Serious bleeding was more frequent only in people also taking blood thinners (3.4% vs 2.6%).
- **Irregular heart rhythm:** **atrial fibrillation** (an irregular, often fast heart rhythm) or flutter occurred in 5.8% vs 4.5%, and in 12.5% vs 6.3% of people who'd had it before.
- **Other common effects:** swelling of the hands or legs, constipation, muscle and joint pain, gout and rash.
- **Allergies:** it's contraindicated with soya allergy, and it shouldn't be used with peanut allergy either. Use caution with fish or shellfish allergy.
- **Hereditary fructose intolerance:** the capsules contain sorbitol and maltitol, so people with this rare inherited condition shouldn't take them.

## The other omega-3 story

Mixed omega-3 medicines, which combine EPA with **DHA** (docosahexaenoic acid, another omega-3 fatty acid) as in Omacor, were authorised in several EU countries from 2000 for use after a heart attack, at 1 g a day. The EMA later concluded they weren't effective for that purpose, and that indication was removed. They're still approved for lowering triglycerides.

The two belong to the same family, but they're different products, at different doses, with different evidence. This module follows that contrast throughout.

## What this module is, and isn't

This is a learning module, not prescribing advice. Vazkepa is under **additional monitoring**, the EU's black-triangle status for medicines whose safety is watched especially closely. The module is refreshed every six months, or immediately if the SmPC changes.

The SmPC gives no revision date of its own, and the leaflet's 'last revised' line is blank.

## From capsule to EPA

Each capsule holds an **ethyl ester** of EPA, a stable chemical form suited to a medicine. During absorption, the gut removes the ethyl group through **de-esterification**, and EPA is taken up in the small intestine.

From there, most of it travels through the **lymphatic system**, the network of vessels that carries absorbed fats, before it reaches the blood. Levels peak about 5 hours after a dose.

In every trial, Vazkepa was taken with or after a meal, and no study checked the effect of food. That's why the SmPC says to take it with food.

## A mechanism that isn't fully understood

The SmPC says plainly that the mechanisms 'are not completely understood'. It lists several that are likely to contribute:

- fewer triglyceride-rich particles in the blood
- anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects
- fewer inflammatory cells (macrophages) in artery walls
- better function of the vessel lining
- more stable plaques
- a mild effect against platelet clumping

One proposed route: EPA takes the place of **arachidonic acid**, another fatty acid in cell membranes. As a result, the body makes fewer of the pro-inflammatory **eicosanoids**, signalling molecules made from these fatty acids. The SmPC adds that the direct clinical meaning of each finding is unclear.

## What it does to blood fats

In the liver, EPA slows the enzymes that build triglycerides and speeds up fat burning. The result is less **VLDL** (very-low-density lipoprotein, the particle that carries triglycerides from the liver). EPA also boosts lipoprotein lipase, the enzyme that clears triglycerides from the blood.

The net effect is lower triglycerides, lower VLDL, lower **remnant cholesterol** (cholesterol carried in the leftovers of triglyceride-rich particles) and lower CRP, a blood marker of inflammation.

## The puzzle

Triglycerides fell by 18%, yet cardiovascular events fell by 25%. According to the SmPC, how much triglycerides or LDL fell had little link to how much benefit a patient got. The EPA level in the blood had a much stronger link: people who reached 175 µg/mL or more had less than half the risk of those below 100 µg/mL. The average at the start was 26 µg/mL.

Keep in mind that this is an **on-treatment analysis**: it compares patients by the levels they happened to reach, not by randomisation. People who reach high levels may differ in other ways, such as how reliably they take their capsules. So the EPA link is suggestive, not proof.

## What happens in the body

Most EPA in the blood is built into larger fat molecules, and less than 1% circulates as a free fatty acid. The body breaks EPA down by **beta-oxidation**, the same fat-burning process it uses for dietary fats. CYP enzymes play only a minor part, and EPA isn't excreted by the kidneys.

The half-life of EPA (the time for blood levels to halve) is about 89 hours, which is long. In interaction studies, icosapent ethyl didn't change levels of omeprazole, rosiglitazone, warfarin or atorvastatin.

## Sources

2. **EPAR-level** — EMA press release on omega-3 fatty acid medicines (post-heart-attack indication).

## The omega-3 backstory

Mixed omega-3 medicines were first approved for use after a heart attack in several EU countries around 2000. The approvals rested largely on GISSI-Prevenzione, a 1999 trial that was **open-label**, meaning patients and doctors knew who was getting what.

Later trials and analyses didn't confirm the benefit. The EMA reviewed all the data and concluded that the benefit–risk balance for preventing further heart problems after a heart attack was negative. That use was removed, although the products can still be used to lower triglycerides. There were no new safety concerns.

## A different product, a new trial

Icosapent ethyl was developed by Amarin as purified EPA only, at a much higher dose of 4 g a day. Its approval didn't rest on the older omega-3 data. It rested on its own outcome trial, REDUCE-IT.

The CHMP gave a positive opinion on 28 January 2021, and the European Commission authorised Vazkepa on 26 March 2021. Great Britain followed the next month.

## The placebo question

REDUCE-IT's placebo capsules contained a small amount of light mineral oil (4 mL). The SmPC notes that this may have had a mild laxative effect, which complicates the comparison for constipation.

There's a second detail. At one year, LDL had risen by 10% on placebo but only 3% on icosapent ethyl. Whether the mineral-oil placebo made the placebo group slightly worse off is a long-running debate, covered in Lesson 8.

## Approval is not access

An EU licence doesn't put a medicine in patients' hands. In most countries it also needs **reimbursement**: national agreement to pay for it, negotiated country by country. Amarin filed about 20 reimbursement dossiers. Sweden granted national reimbursement and launch in March 2022, and Finland reimbursed it in October 2022, with launch in December. Some countries, such as Denmark, allow reimbursement for individual patients before a national decision.

## 2025: the Recordati deal

On 24 June 2025, Amarin signed an exclusive long-term **licensing agreement**, including supply, with Recordati covering 59 countries, mostly in Europe. The terms:

- $25 million upfront
- up to $150 million in **milestone payments**, sums due when agreed sales levels are reached
- ongoing supply revenue and royalties

Amarin said its European patent protection runs to 2039, and it restructured its operations to save about $70 million. Recordati is now the marketing authorisation holder, and its affiliates are the local contacts across Europe.

## Renewal

The licence was renewed on 15 January 2026, and Vazkepa remains under additional monitoring. Vazkepa isn't authorised for children, and the EMA waived paediatric studies for it.

5. **Secondary** — World Pharmaceuticals (2025), for the timing of the Great Britain approval.

## One indication, several gates

Vazkepa has a single indication, and a patient has to meet every part of it:

1. An adult
2. Already taking a statin. Vazkepa is an **adjunct**, meaning it's added on top of the statin, not used instead of it.
3. At high cardiovascular risk
4. With triglycerides of 1.7 mmol/L or higher
5. With either established cardiovascular disease, or diabetes plus at least one other **risk factor**, meaning a feature that raises the chance of a heart attack or stroke

If any part is missing, the patient falls outside the licence.

## What REDUCE-IT meant by high risk

The trial behind the indication enrolled two groups:

- **Established cardiovascular disease** (71%): aged 45 or over, with documented disease of the heart arteries, the brain or neck arteries, or the leg arteries
- **Diabetes plus risk factors** (29%): aged 50 or over, with diabetes treated with medicines, plus at least one of these:
  - high blood pressure
  - older age (55 or over for men, 65 or over for women)
  - low HDL cholesterol
  - smoking
  - raised CRP (a marker of inflammation)
  - kidney impairment
  - protein in the urine
  - diabetic eye disease
  - signs of narrowed leg arteries

The SmPC points to these definitions in section 5.1.

## Label and trial don't match exactly

The trial's **entry criteria**, the rules for who could join, differed from the label in two ways:

- **Triglycerides:** the trial accepted patients from 1.53 mmol/L at screening (up to just under 5.64). The label starts at 1.7 mmol/L.
- **LDL:** the trial required LDL that was already fairly well controlled on a statin, between 1.03 and 2.59 mmol/L. The label doesn't state an LDL range.

Both gaps are normal: a label is written for practice, not as a copy of the trial protocol. But it's worth knowing that patients with high LDL weren't studied.

## Notice what isn't there

- **A triglyceride indication:** Vazkepa isn't licensed simply to lower triglycerides.
- **Use without a statin:** everyone in REDUCE-IT took a statin.
- **Children:** paediatric studies were waived.
- **Very high triglycerides:** levels of 5.64 mmol/L or above were excluded from the trial.
- **PCSK9 inhibitor users:** they were excluded from the trial.

## The Omacor comparison

Mixed omega-3 (Omacor) now has a different, purely lipid indication: endogenous hypertriglyceridaemia (raised triglycerides produced by the body, rather than from dietary fat), alongside diet. The **Fredrickson types** are an older laboratory classification of lipid disorders, and Omacor's indication uses them:

- **Type IV** (triglycerides raised): Omacor on its own.
- **Types IIb and III** (cholesterol and triglycerides both raised): Omacor with a statin, when the statin doesn't control triglycerides well enough.

It isn't for type I, where the raised triglycerides come from dietary fat. Its old heart indication after a heart attack was removed.

3. **SmPC (comparison)** — Omacor 1000 mg soft capsules, Spanish SmPC (CIMA 65476), section 4.1.

## A large capsule, four times a day

Vazkepa comes in a single strength: a 998 mg **soft capsule**, meaning a gelatin shell filled with liquid. It's oblong, light yellow to amber, 25 × 10 mm, and printed 'IPE' in white.

The **excipients**, the ingredients other than the active substance, that patients need to know about are:

- maltitol (30 mg) and sorbitol (83 mg), both sugar alcohols
- soya lecithin

The daily dose is four capsules. For people who find tablets hard to swallow, that's a real consideration.

## Packs designed for the dose

- **Bottles:** 120 capsules, which at four a day is 30 days' supply. Cartons hold one or three bottles. The cap is child-resistant: push down and turn.
- **Blisters:** unit-dose strips of 4×2 capsules, printed 'Day 1 · Dose 1 · Dose 2', to make the twice-daily routine easier to follow.

The capsules keep for five years when stored below 30 °C and protected from moisture.

## Who stands behind it

The **MAH** (marketing authorisation holder, the company legally responsible for the product) is Recordati in Milan. Batches are released by MIAS Pharma in Ireland.

The **local representative**, the company patients and doctors contact in each country, is almost always a Recordati affiliate: Bouchara-Recordati in France, Casen Recordati in Spain, Jaba Recordati in Portugal, and Herbacos Recordati in the Czech Republic and Slovakia. The exception is Greece, where the partner Vianex fills that role.

## Same code, different evidence

The **ATC code** is the international classification that groups medicines by chemistry and use. Vazkepa and Omacor share the same one: C10AX06.

Yet one has outcome evidence for heart protection, and the other lost its heart indication. An ATC code classifies a molecule's chemistry, not the evidence for using it, so the same code can carry very different labels.

## The comparison product

Omacor comes as 1 g soft capsules, each containing 460 mg of EPA and 380 mg of DHA (as ethyl esters), plus vitamin E as an antioxidant. It also contains soya oil. The dose is two capsules a day, rising to four if needed. Bottles hold 20 to 100 capsules, and there's also a 10 × 28 multipack.

## Sources

1. **SmPC** — Vazkepa, EU SmPC. Sections 2, 3, 5.1, 6, 7; Annex II; package leaflet section 6.
2. **SmPC (comparison)** — Omacor 1000 mg, Spanish SmPC and PIL (CIMA 65476); UK SmPC (emc product 1706).

## The routine

The dose is two capsules twice a day, taken with or just after a meal. Swallow them whole: don't break, crush, dissolve or chew them, so the full dose gets through.

All the trials gave it with food, and no study tested it without food. That's why the meal instruction matters.

## A missed dose

Take a missed dose as soon as you remember. If a whole day's dose is missed, just carry on with the next scheduled dose. Don't double up to catch up.

## Kidneys, liver and age

No dose change is needed for kidney or liver impairment, or for age. The pharmacokinetics haven't been studied in kidney or liver impairment, but REDUCE-IT patients with these conditions didn't need routine dose changes.

In people with liver impairment, the SmPC asks for liver enzymes (ALT and AST) to be checked before starting and at suitable intervals during treatment.

## Bleeding and heart rhythm

**Bleeding:** if someone also takes antiplatelet medicines (including aspirin) or anticoagulants, monitor them periodically. If signs of bleeding appear, such as bruising, nosebleeds, blood in the urine or gut bleeding, appropriate laboratory tests may be considered. Patients should report any bleeding promptly.

**Heart rhythm:** watch for atrial fibrillation, especially in people who've had it before. Signs include palpitations, breathlessness, fainting or dizziness, chest discomfort and an irregular pulse. Do an ECG when clinically indicated.

## Allergies and sugars

- **Soya or peanut allergy:** don't use it, because the capsule contains soya lecithin.
- **Fish or shellfish allergy:** use with caution. It isn't known whether the risk is higher.
- **Hereditary fructose intolerance:** don't use it, because of the sorbitol and maltitol.
- **Other medicines:** sorbitol adds to any sorbitol or fructose from other medicines or food, and may affect how well some other oral medicines are absorbed.

## Pregnancy and breastfeeding: three wordings

**Pregnancy:** there are limited data. As a precaution, it's better to avoid Vazkepa unless the benefit outweighs the risk to the baby.

**Breastfeeding:** the sources say different things:

- The Vazkepa SmPC says to decide between stopping breastfeeding and stopping Vazkepa, weighing the benefit of each. EPA passes into breast milk in line with the mother's diet.
- The Vazkepa PIL simply says it's 'not recommended'.
- The UK Omacor SmPC says it 'should not be used' during breastfeeding.

The Vazkepa SmPC is the reference here.

## Children, driving and overdose

- **Children:** there's no relevant use under 18.
- **Driving:** Vazkepa has no or negligible effect on driving or using machines.
- **Overdose:** there's no specific treatment. Treat the symptoms and give supportive care.

## Why this lesson comes first

The omega-3 story turns on questions that most trials let you skip: what was the placebo made of, why did one trial stop early and another not, and why do two similar-looking trials disagree? This lesson covers those questions before Lesson 8 applies them.

## A placebo is still a **comparator**

Every result compares the drug with something else, its comparator. Ideally that comparator is an **inert placebo**: a dummy that has no effect of its own.

For oil-based capsules, though, the placebo has to be an oil too. REDUCE-IT used light mineral oil, and STRENGTH used corn oil. If the placebo oil isn't truly inert, the result measures the drug's effect *plus* any harm or benefit from the placebo.

## What happened in REDUCE-IT's placebo arm

At one year, LDL had risen by 10% in the placebo arm, compared with 3% on icosapent ethyl (SmPC figures). Reports of the trial data also describe rises in CRP (an inflammation marker) and apolipoprotein B in the placebo arm.

In STRENGTH, the corn-oil placebo didn't change these **biomarkers** (lab measures used to track a biological process). That's the core of the debate: was part of REDUCE-IT's benefit really the mineral-oil group doing slightly worse?

## How big could the placebo effect be?

No one knows exactly. The investigators of STRENGTH argued that at least part of REDUCE-IT's benefit may come from more events in the control arm. Supporters of REDUCE-IT point out that the shifts in placebo biomarkers were small, and that analyses within the trial still showed a substantial effect.

The EMA approved Vazkepa on REDUCE-IT and presents its efficacy in the SmPC. The SmPC mentions mineral oil only when discussing constipation. Commentators have called for a head-to-head trial, or another corn-oil-controlled trial.

## Stopping early for futility

Trials can be stopped early for benefit (as with rosuvastatin's JUPITER) or **stopped for futility**: when an interim look shows the trial is very unlikely to find a benefit if it continues. That decision rests with the independent **data monitoring committee**, the experts who review the results while the trial is still blinded to everyone else.

STRENGTH was stopped for futility in January 2020. Its two event curves were almost on top of each other.

## Five-point and three-point MACE

REDUCE-IT's primary endpoint counted five event types: cardiovascular death, heart attack, stroke, artery-opening procedures and hospitalisation for unstable angina.

Its key secondary endpoint counted only the three 'hardest' ones: cardiovascular death, heart attack and stroke. Both fell by about a quarter, so the result didn't rest only on the softer events.

## When trials disagree

REDUCE-IT and STRENGTH differ in several ways at once: the product (purified EPA vs EPA plus DHA), the placebo (mineral oil vs corn oil), the patients (STRENGTH required low HDL) and how much EPA levels rose. This is **between-trial heterogeneity**: differences in design that make it impossible to pin the difference in results on any one cause.

Secondary sources don't even agree on the EPA figures. One summary reports a rise of 144 vs 90 µg/mL; another reports 63% vs 67%. When summaries conflict, go back to the original paper.

## Open-label then, blinded now

The older omega-3 approvals rested on GISSI-Prevenzione (1999), which was open-label: patients and doctors knew who took what. REDUCE-IT and STRENGTH were both double-blind. Their disagreement is about the details of good trials, not about one good trial and one poor one.

## The combination tags

Each trial card carries exactly one tag:

- MONO: no background lipid-lowering treatment
- 🔗 +STATIN: everyone on a statin
- 🔗 +STATIN+EZE: on a statin plus ezetimibe
- 🔗 +EZE: on ezetimibe
- 🔗 +PCSK9: on a PCSK9 inhibitor
- 🔗 +ANTIHTN: on blood-pressure medicines
- 🔗 +SGLT2: on an SGLT2 inhibitor
- 🔗 +GLP1: on a GLP-1 receptor agonist
- 🔗 FDC: a combination tablet
- 🔗 MIXED: varied background treatment

cards.back: What the drug is compared against. For oil capsules, the placebo is an oil too: mineral oil in REDUCE-IT, corn oil in STRENGTH.
In REDUCE-IT's placebo arm, LDL rose 10% (vs 3% on the drug), and CRP and apoB also rose. Was part of the benefit placebo harm? The question is unresolved.
Ended early because a benefit had become very unlikely. STRENGTH was stopped in January 2020.
Differences in product, placebo, patients and EPA levels between trials. They make the cause of differing results hard to pin down.

questions.stem: Why can't REDUCE-IT vs STRENGTH be read as a clean comparison of EPA vs EPA+DHA?
options: Because STRENGTH was open-label
Because the trials differed in product, placebo oil, patients and EPA levels all at once
Because REDUCE-IT was too small
Because both had the same result

3. **Secondary** — Cleveland Clinic ConsultQD; PACE-CME; R3i editorial; MDedge and Pharmaceutical Technology reports of the STRENGTH presentation (AHA 2020).
4. **EPAR-level** — EMA press release on omega-3 fatty acid medicines (GISSI-Prevenzione).

## One pivotal trial, one key contrast

The EU licence rests on a single **pivotal trial**, REDUCE-IT. A second trial is just as important for understanding the evidence: STRENGTH, which tested a different high-dose omega-3 product and found no benefit.

Both tags are 🔗 +STATIN, because every patient in both trials was on a statin.

### Trial card: REDUCE-IT
Tag: 🔗 +STATIN

- Registry: NCT01492361
- Who took part: 8,179 statin-treated adults: 70.7% with established cardiovascular disease, and 29.3% with diabetes plus risk factors. Triglycerides were 1.53 to under 5.64 mmol/L at screening, LDL 1.03–2.59 mmol/L. Median age 64; 28.8% women; 90% White.
- Background therapy: a moderate- (63%) or high-intensity (31%) statin. Most also took antiplatelets (85.5%) and blood-pressure medicines (95.2%). PCSK9 inhibitors were excluded.
- Compared with: a light mineral-oil placebo, randomised 1:1, event-driven, median 4.9 years
- Main question: does icosapent ethyl 4 g a day reduce five-point MACE?
- Headline result: 17.2% vs 22.0%, HR 0.75 (95% CI 0.68–0.83), p < 0.0001: 25% lower in relative terms and 4.8 percentage points in absolute terms. Three-point MACE: 11.2% vs 14.8%, HR 0.74.
- In plain words: on top of a statin, icosapent ethyl cut major heart events by about a quarter over five years.
- Worth knowing: the placebo arm's LDL rose 10% (vs 3% on the drug), and other placebo-arm biomarkers also rose, which is the mineral-oil debate. Hospitalisation for atrial fibrillation was more frequent (3% vs 2%).

### Trial card: STRENGTH
Tag: 🔗 +STATIN

- Registry: NCT02104817
- Who took part: 13,078 statin-treated adults at high cardiovascular risk, with raised triglycerides (180–500 mg/dL) and low HDL. 675 centres in 22 countries.
- Background therapy: a statin, plus usual care
- Compared with: a corn-oil placebo, randomised 1:1. Stopped for futility in January 2020.
- Main question: does omega-3 carboxylic acids 4 g a day (EPA plus DHA, Epanova) reduce five-point MACE?
- Headline result: 12.0% vs 12.2%, HR 0.99 (95% CI 0.90–1.09), p = 0.84: no difference in relative or absolute terms.
- In plain words: a high-dose EPA-plus-DHA product didn't reduce heart events compared with corn oil.
- Worth knowing: triglycerides fell 19% and CRP 20%, yet outcomes didn't change. Atrial fibrillation increased, by about 69% in relative terms. Epanova isn't one of the products covered in this module.

blocks.markdown:
## How to hold these two results

These aren't a head-to-head comparison. Product, placebo, patients (STRENGTH required low HDL) and EPA levels all differed, so no single explanation can be proven.

The main candidate explanations are:

1. EPA alone works, but adding DHA doesn't.
2. A higher EPA level is needed.
3. Part of REDUCE-IT's effect came from the mineral-oil placebo.

Each has supporters. The EU licence is built on REDUCE-IT, and Lesson 14 shows how guidelines handle the uncertainty.

## The older omega-3 trials

For the mixed omega-3 products, the original heart approval rested on GISSI-Prevenzione (1999), an open-label trial of 1 g a day. Later randomised trials and meta-analyses didn't confirm the benefit, which led the EMA to remove that indication.

OMEMI tested 1.8 g a day of EPA plus DHA against corn oil in 1,027 people aged 70–82 who'd recently had a heart attack. After two years it found no reduction in events (21.4% vs 20.0%, HR 1.08). New atrial fibrillation was more frequent on the omega-3 (7.2% vs 4.0%), though this difference wasn't statistically significant.

cards.back: 8,179 statin-treated patients, 4.9 years, mineral-oil placebo. Five-point MACE 17.2% vs 22.0%, HR 0.75.
13,078 patients, EPA+DHA 4 g a day vs corn oil. 12.0% vs 12.2%, HR 0.99. Stopped for futility.
EPA alone works but DHA doesn't add benefit; a higher EPA level is needed; or the mineral-oil placebo inflated the effect. None is proven.

## Always a combination

Icosapent ethyl is never used on its own. Its licence requires a statin, and in REDUCE-IT nearly everyone also took blood-pressure and antiplatelet medicines. This lesson looks at six partners: **statins**, **ezetimibe**, **PCSK9 inhibitors**, **blood-pressure medicines**, **SGLT2 inhibitors** and **GLP-1 receptor agonists**.

The main source here is REDUCE-IT's background therapy. No dedicated combination trials were found for any of the six partners.

## What the licence names

The Vazkepa indication names one partner: a statin. It's required ('statin-treated patients'). None of the other five partners is mentioned, and none is excluded either. No combination tablet containing icosapent ethyl exists in the EU.

## What the SmPC says about partners

- **Statins:** no change in drug levels with atorvastatin.
- **Other medicines processed by liver enzymes:** no interaction with omeprazole, rosiglitazone (a diabetes medicine) or warfarin.
- **Antiplatelets and anticoagulants:** higher bleeding risk, so monitor periodically.
- **Ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors, blood-pressure medicines, SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists:** no lines at all.

The sorbitol in the capsule may affect how well some other oral medicines are absorbed, but that applies to medicines in general, not to any specific partner.

## How to read the six columns

All six columns come from the background therapy in one trial, not from trials designed to test each combination. Read each column on its own, never as a ranking.

- **Statins and blood-pressure medicines** are well represented, because nearly every patient took them.
- **Ezetimibe** is thin, at 6.4% of patients.
- **PCSK9 inhibitors** are absent, because they were excluded.
- **SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists** are rare, because the trial predates their widespread use.

## How REDUCE-IT handled ezetimibe

The trial used **stratified randomisation**: patients were randomised separately within groups, one of which was whether they took ezetimibe, so that each arm received a balanced share of ezetimibe users. The investigators reported no difference in benefit between patients who did and didn't take ezetimibe.

With only about 520 ezetimibe users, though, the trial couldn't have detected a modest difference. 'No difference seen' isn't the same as 'shown to be the same'.

## Why PCSK9 inhibitors were excluded

Patients on PCSK9 inhibitors could join only after a **washout**, meaning they stopped the drug for a set period before enrolment. In practice, that kept PCSK9 users out of the trial.

So for someone on a statin plus a PCSK9 inhibitor whose triglycerides are still high, REDUCE-IT provides no direct evidence.

### Trial card: REDUCE-IT, patients with diabetes
Tag: 🔗 +STATIN

- Registry: NCT01492361
- Who took part: REDUCE-IT patients with type 2 diabetes, 4,730 (57.8%) of the 8,179
- Background therapy: a statin for everyone. Only a small proportion took SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists.
- Compared with: the mineral-oil placebo, median follow-up 4.9 years (a prespecified subgroup analysis)
- Main question: does the benefit hold in people with diabetes?
- Headline result: for the primary endpoint, HR 0.77 vs placebo. Absolute rates weren't in the sources reviewed. The **subgroup interaction**, the test of whether benefit differed with or without diabetes, wasn't significant (p = 0.29).
- In plain words: people with diabetes benefited about as much as everyone else in the trial.
- Worth knowing: this is the closest evidence for the SGLT2 and GLP-1 columns. It doesn't test those combinations, because few patients took those medicines.

## The question

Does icosapent ethyl reduce heart attacks, strokes and deaths? The EU answer rests on REDUCE-IT: 8,179 statin-treated patients followed for a median of 4.9 years.

In short, it reduced both composite endpoints and almost every individual event, including cardiovascular death. Death from any cause fell too, but not significantly.

## Event by event

- **Heart attack:** 6.1% vs 8.7% (HR 0.69). That's 31% lower in relative terms and 2.6 percentage points lower in absolute terms.
- **Stroke:** 2.4% vs 3.3% (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.55–0.93), 0.9 points lower.
- **Urgent or emergency artery-opening procedure:** 5.3% vs 7.8% (HR 0.65), 2.5 points lower.
- **Hospitalisation for unstable angina:** 2.6% vs 3.8% (HR 0.68), 1.2 points lower.

Unlike bempedoic acid in CLEAR Outcomes, the effect here includes stroke.

## Deaths

- **Cardiovascular death:** 4.3% vs 5.2% (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.66–0.98). That's 20% lower in relative terms and 0.9 points lower in absolute terms.
- **Death from any cause:** 6.7% vs 7.6% (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.74–1.02). Not significant.

The SmPC notes that death from any cause wasn't part of either composite endpoint. It was reported, but the trial wasn't designed to test it.

## Turning it into people

The primary endpoint fell from 22.0% to 17.2%, a difference of 4.8 percentage points. On those figures, about 21 people would need treating for around 4.9 years to prevent one event. That's the **number needed to treat**, calculated here from the published rates.

Don't set it against other modules' NNTs, such as about 63 for bempedoic acid. Different trials, patients, follow-up times and placebos make that comparison meaningless.

## Consistent across subgroups, with one twist

The benefit was similar across the prespecified subgroups: primary vs secondary prevention, diabetes or not, men vs women, and US vs non-US patients (all interaction p-values above 0.29).

The twist: the benefit was similar whether baseline triglycerides were above or below 1.7 mmol/L (150 mg/dL) (p = 0.68), even though the label's threshold is 1.7. That fits Lesson 2's point that triglycerides aren't the main driver.

In the 3,146 patients from the US, the reduction looked larger (HR 0.69), and it included death from any cause. The difference between regions wasn't statistically significant, but it has fed the debate over the mineral-oil placebo.

## The headline list

The SmPC lists the most frequent side effects as:

- bleeding (11.8%)
- swelling of the hands or legs (7.8%)
- atrial fibrillation (5.8%)
- constipation (5.4%)
- muscle and bone pain (4.3%)
- gout (4.3%)
- rash (3.0%)

The frequencies come from all trials plus reports received after launch.

## By frequency

- **Very common:** bleeding
- **Common:** atrial fibrillation or flutter, constipation, **eructation** (burping), gout, rash, muscle and bone pain, and swelling of the hands or legs
- **Uncommon:** allergic reactions, and **dysgeusia**, an altered sense of taste (a fishy taste here)
- **Not known:** swelling of the throat

Reports received since launch also mention raised triglycerides, joint pain, diarrhoea, abdominal discomfort and pain in the arms or legs. These come from voluntary reports, so neither their frequency nor a causal link can be established.

## Bleeding: it depends on the partners

Bleeding occurred in 11.8% vs 9.9% on placebo. The most frequent types were gut bleeding (3.1%), bruising (2.5%), blood in the urine (1.9%) and nosebleeds (1.5%).

Serious bleeding was more frequent only in people also taking an **antithrombotic**, a medicine that prevents clots, such as aspirin or an anticoagulant: 3.4% vs 2.6%. Without one, the rate was 0.2% in both groups.

blocks.markdown:
## Atrial fibrillation: a class signal

Atrial fibrillation or flutter occurred in 5.8% vs 4.5%. It needed hospitalisation of 24 hours or more in 3% vs 2%. In people who'd had it before, the rate doubled: 12.5% vs 6.3%.

The signal isn't unique to icosapent ethyl. STRENGTH (EPA+DHA) showed about a 69% relative increase in atrial fibrillation, and OMEMI saw more of it too (7.2% vs 4.0%), though that difference wasn't statistically significant. The STRENGTH lead investigator described it as a concern across omega-3 trials.

## Constipation, and the placebo again

Constipation occurred in 5.4% vs 3.6%. Serious constipation was rare: 0.1% vs 0.2%.

The SmPC itself warns that this comparison may be confounded. The mineral-oil placebo may have had a mild laxative effect, which would make constipation look more common on the medicine than it really is.

## When to contact a doctor

The patient leaflet tells patients to contact a doctor straight away about:

- palpitations or an irregular heartbeat, which can mean atrial fibrillation
- bruising easily, or bleeding that won't stop

They should also get medical help for an allergic reaction:

- rash or itching
- hives
- difficulty breathing
- tightness in the throat
- swollen lips
- stomach cramps, diarrhoea or vomiting

lessons.title: Who shouldn't take it, and interactions

blocks.markdown:
## Contraindications

Vazkepa must not be used in anyone allergic to icosapent ethyl, to soya, or to any other ingredient. The SmPC adds that people allergic to peanut must not use it either, because the capsule contains soya lecithin.

People with hereditary fructose intolerance shouldn't take it, because it contains maltitol and sorbitol.

## Use with care

- **Fish or shellfish allergy:** use with caution. It isn't known whether the risk of an allergic reaction is higher.
- **Liver impairment:** monitor ALT and AST before starting and during treatment.
- **History of atrial fibrillation:** watch for symptoms, and do an ECG when clinically indicated.
- **Antithrombotic medicines:** bleeding risk is higher, so monitor periodically.

## Interactions: a short list

EPA is cleared mainly by beta-oxidation, the same process the body uses for dietary fats. CYP enzymes play only a minor role, which keeps the interaction potential low.

When icosapent ethyl was tested at the full dose with four medicines that are typical CYP substrates (omeprazole, rosiglitazone, warfarin and atorvastatin), no interactions were seen.

The practical interaction isn't about drug levels at all. It's added bleeding risk with antiplatelet medicines (including aspirin) and anticoagulants.

## Sorbitol: the excipient interaction

Each capsule contains 83 mg of sorbitol, so a full day's dose contains about 332 mg. The SmPC asks prescribers to take into account sorbitol or fructose from other medicines and from food. It also notes that sorbitol may affect how well some other oral medicines are absorbed.
